description:
Veylith is an independent, research-driven team participating in the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge in Raleigh, North Carolina.

Our interests lie at the intersection of artificial intelligence, statistical modeling, Earth observation, and sustainable agriculture. We aim to explore how NASA's open scientific datasets can be transformed into practical, accessible tools that address real-world challenges.
summary:
The farmer may decide what to plant, but he or she cannot decide what the coming season holds. With growing droughts, increasingly unpredictable precipitation, and deteriorating soil, what may work now may fail later. Farmers do not only require guidance on what to do; they need to know when they can trust the guidance.

That is where Hinge comes in, a crop rotation decision tool powered by NASA and based on satellite observations of the environment.

Hinge combines NASA POWER climate data, Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 imagery, USDA soil data, and agricultural research in order to evaluate realistic crop rotations based on decades of environmental variability. Farmers can compare options, examine trade-offs, and understand how changes in precipitation, soil conditions, planting times, or priorities affect their optimal rotation.

The key innovation in Hinge is our Decision Boundary Engine: Hinge does not just rank rotations; Hinge explains why a particular rotation is recommended, under what circumstances it becomes impractical, and what facts the farmer needs to confirm before implementing the recommendation.

We do not try to predict the future. We try to help farmers make informed decisions in an uncertain world.
details:
HINGE is a decision support tool based on interactive data that has been built to assist farmers in modifying their crop rotations due to changes in environmental conditions. This product was created as part of NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, specifically Field Shift: Adapt Farms With NASA Data, by combining data from Earth observation by NASA, historical weather data, soil information by USDA, and crop requirements. HINGE allows users to view the best decision under varying priorities and environmental conditions, rather than dictating the best option for everyone.

HINGE integrates many kinds of environmental data ranging from the NASA POWER meteorological data to the NASA HLS vegetation data, as well as the USDA soil data. The dashboard of HINGE's Farm Intelligence shows environmental conditions, weather patterns, soil characteristics, and vegetation trends in an integrated way.

With the help of the Rotation Comparison feature of the HINGE, it becomes possible to analyze different crop rotation alternatives for various historical periods of weather. Users can adjust parameters and define such goals as minimizing deficit of water requirements by crops or reducing rainfall effects when there is low soil coverage. HINGE calculates the outcomes and compares them.

There is also feasibility checking on the platform in order to exclude unsuitable agricultural practices based on environmental restrictions. There is also the synthetic demonstration mode which allows exploring various hypotheses without mixing simulations with environmental data.

The mission of HINGE is to enable farmers, agricultural scientists, and educators to access and utilize environmental information through an understandable and user-friendly interface. HINGE brings together a number of data sources to create a comprehensive decision-making tool that enables users to balance water resources, soil conservation, climate change, and crop selection.

In the long run, it is intended to encourage climate-resilient agriculture by empowering farmers to implement water-saving measures, protect their soil, and adapt to unpredictable weather conditions. HINGE is designed to facilitate decision-making processes but does not substitute the local knowledge of farmers or guarantee any agricultural results.

The creation of HINGE was completed in web app form using React, TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML, and CSS along with Vite. Environmental data processing, scientific analysis, and validation were done using Python. The scientific aspects of the project were done using NASA POWER, NASA HLS data, along with USDA soil data.

Version control and collaboration for the project were done via GitHub, while data processing and validation were done in Google Colab. Vercel was used for deploying the web app. Scientific validation and automated tests were done in order to check the accuracy and replicability of calculations and data.

The innovations in HINGE rely on an objective-based approach to agriculture. In contrast with systems which offer a certain optimal plan for decision making, HINGE demonstrates the variability of the most advantageous crop rotation depending on the objective chosen for the optimization process.

So, for example, while the rotation which proves to be the best one for the reduction of unfulfilled water demand may not necessarily correspond to the optimal choice in case of the highest priority of soil protection during rainfall periods.

In this way, HINGE makes visible and interactive the process of decision making in agriculture. The system divides scientifically substantiated calculation from artificial demonstrations of the results of calculations.

At all stages of development, our team kept the notions of scientific precision, openness, accessibility, and agricultural relevancy in the center of our concerns. We took into account the fact that the environmental data is different in its coverage, the historical climate variations, the soil conditions, the water limitations, and the uncertainty of the assumptions used within the models.

Moreover, our goal is to ensure that the application will not show modeled results as certain facts of reality. The main aspects to take into account were the data source, reproducible processing, simulation labeling, and feasibility restrictions.

Last but not least, the HINGE is designed in a way that allows us to present scientific notions in a visual appealing way. The point is not to provide the data provided by NASA but to make it understandable for further comparisons and making agricultural decisions based on these data.
